hypotheses.claim: JSON serialization dominates the non‑SQL latency
hypotheses.mechanism: After the DTO list is built, Jackson (or the configured JSON mapper) writes each CustomerDto to a byte buffer; the time grows ≈7 ms per KB of output (measured from the sweep: 142 KB → 1092 ms, 418 KB → 3173 ms, 658 KB → 5309 ms, giving ~6.7‑7.0 ms/KB). This accounts for most of the 88 % non‑SQL time.
evidence: page_size=1 → body 142 297 B, latency 1091.8 ms, non‑SQL ≈ 983 ms
page_size=5 → body 418 458 B, latency 3172.8 ms, non‑SQL ≈ 2798 ms
page_size=20 → body 657 650 B, latency 5309.1 ms, non‑SQL ≈ 4612 ms
hypotheses.prediction: If the response is sent as plain text or compressed JSON (reducing body size), the latency will drop proportionally, even with the same number of rows.

hypotheses.claim: Per‑row application‑logic (DTO construction & invoice aggregation) adds a fixed cost per result row
hypotheses.mechanism: CustomerService.enrich creates a CustomerDto and calls InvoiceService.getOutstanding, which runs a SUM query (already measured) and then performs Java calculations; the number of SQL statements per request rises with rows (4 → 12 → 42) while SQL time stays ~10 % of total, implying the remaining per‑row work (object allocation, loops) consumes ≈20 ms per row (≈200 ms for 10‑row request).
evidence: application SQL statements per request: 4 (1 row), 12 (5 rows), 42 (20 rows)
SQL time per request: 108 ms, 375 ms, 697 ms (≈10 % of latency)
hypotheses.prediction: If DTO construction is bypassed (e.g., returning only IDs), latency will decrease roughly by 20 ms per row regardless of body size.

hypotheses.claim: ORM hydration of Customer entities and lazy collections adds modest overhead
hypotheses.mechanism: Hibernate loads each Customer row (≈1.6 M rows sent) and, for every row, triggers a lazy collection fetch that issues another query (Customer.getInvoices). These entity materialisations are not reflected in the SQL timing because they are cheap, but they cause allocator and GC pressure, contributing ~5 % of latency.
evidence: rows examined / rows sent: 5 110 057 / 1 649 126 indicates many extra rows processed
two digests report ‘no index used’, suggesting full scans for lazy loads
hypotheses.prediction: Setting hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size > 0 or eager‑fetching invoices will reduce latency by ≈50 ms per request.

probes_run.result: Latency and body size grow together; SQL time stays ~10 % – supports h1 > h2 > h3
Latency increase roughly proportional to body bytes (≈7 ms/KB) more than to statement count alone – favors h1
Same pattern persists at larger scale, confirming serialization cost dominates
Zero rows, tiny body (347 B) and latency 16.4 ms, showing fixed overhead is minimal
